title: Automatic Trophy Data Entry: What Still Needs Checking
description: See which parts of trophy data entry Trophy Guru assists with, which decisions need a person, and how to handle uncertain names, years and missing records.
html:
Automatic trophy data entry is useful when it reduces the work between a photograph and a checked winner record. It becomes risky when a proposed reading is mistaken for a confirmed historical fact. The practical approach is to let the software suggest the text and keep a reviewer responsible for the final interpretation.

Define a record before you enter it

At minimum, a winner record needs the trophy or competition, the year and the winner’s name as supported by the source. Those details are related: a correct name entered against the wrong cup is still a wrong record. Identify the trophy before uploading close-up photographs of its lettering.

Keep the source images together for that trophy. Photograph context as well as text, so the reviewer can tell which engraved band or plate an entry came from. Where an inscription continues around a curve, overlap the images.

What the software can propose

Trophy Guru uses an uploaded set of source photographs to propose names and years. You can review and edit those readings in the private archive, add missing winners from other club evidence, and confirm the resulting records. The aim is to reduce retyping while keeping the original evidence available for checking.

The service does not guarantee that all lettering will be read or that every proposed name is correct. Reflections, wear and unusual scripts can leave the source ambiguous. A second photograph may be more useful than repeatedly accepting a plausible-looking result.

A worked review example

Suppose a fictional trophy appears to show “1964 — A. Macdonald”, but glare hides the first letter of the surname. The software proposes “A. Macdonald”. That proposal does not resolve the glare. The reviewer should examine another angle or a supporting club record before confirming it.

If an honours book clearly gives the winner, record the correction and keep a reference to that source in the project notes. If the evidence remains unclear, leave the question open. This example illustrates a review decision; it is not a measured transcription result or a claim about a real club.

Review these details every time

  • Year: compare each digit, especially where a scratch could resemble a stroke.
  • Name: check initials, punctuation, similar letters and unusual local spellings.
  • Competition: make sure the entry belongs to the right trophy and division.
  • Coverage: check whether all engraved areas have been photographed.
  • Gaps: distinguish missing evidence from a confirmed year without a competition.
  • Identity: do not merge two people solely because they share initials or a surname.

Measure useful progress

Count reviewed entries and unresolved questions, not only the number of rows generated. Include photography and correction time when estimating the project. There is no sound basis for promising that every cabinet will take an afternoon or that a certain number of trophies will take a fixed number of hours.

Once the club has checked the records, export a CSV copy and decide whether they are ready for a public honours board. Retain the source photographs separately as part of the club’s archive arrangements.
